title: Free a pull saw pinched in a branch being cut on two supports
instruction: The saw has got stuck in the branch. Get it out and lay it on the bench.
context: Silky's user guide says: "Occasionally a branch or piece of timber will close around the blade and pinch it." It tells you to "take the load off the blade and relieve the pressure that is trapping it", then "carefully withdraw the saw", and warns "do not wrench the handle from side to side" because the thin pull-saw blade snaps. Branch cutting is regular work for 1,192,500 US landscaping and groundskeeping workers (BLS OOH, 2024) and a common yard job. The careless route is to wrench or yank the saw, which breaks the blade or drags the branch off its supports.
real_product: Silky Gomboy 240-10 folding pull saw. Retail listings (knivesandtools Gomboy 240-10; galaxus; optics-trade) give a 240 mm blade, 270 mm closed, about 500-505 mm open and about 270 g. Blade thickness is not published. The blade cuts on the pull stroke only (Silky instruction sheet, images.toolsid.com/silky-saws/info/pdf/instruction-sheet.pdf). The pinch and its fix come from the Silky Saw User Guide (japanesetools.com.au/blogs/the-jta-blog/silky-saw-user-guide), quoted above. Pinch geometry comes from Husqvarna's "how to stop a chainsaw from pinching" and the Dolmar/Milwaukee bucking pages: with a log supported at both ends "the pressure will be on the top side", and with a log supported at one end "the pressure will be at the underside". So a TOP cut on an overhang opens its kerf. The idea's stated fault (a top cut next to a sawhorse with the outer end overhanging, where the overhang's weight closes the kerf) is physically backwards. The saw itself neither removes the fault nor forces the skill, but the fault only exists in two layouts: a top cut between two supports, or an undercut on a cantilever (in-tree 3-cut pruning). SimReady has no pruning saw. The only saw prop is instrument_handsaw_a01, a carpenter's handsaw measuring 34.7 x 9.8 x 1.2 cm with an authored mass of 0.94 kg. A thin-kerf contact would need a primitive blade collider in either case.
fault: Corrected geometry: a 7 cm green branch rests on two supports and has been top-cut about 80% through between them. The span sags about the uncut fibres, the top of the kerf closes, and the blade is gripped. (The original idea had the overhang beside a sawhorse; that layout cannot pinch a top cut.)
skill: Intended: one hand lifts the branch next to the cut to take the sag load off the kerf, while the other draws the saw out in the plane of the cut without twisting it. Statics show this is not forced. The sag moment at tabletop scale is (0.08*0.97 + 0.06*1.11)*9.81/2 = 0.71 N m, giving a pinch of about 16 N with the blade bearing 4.5 cm above the hinge. Lifting the saw straight up in its own plane carries the cut region with it. About 6.4 N of lift at the cut cancels the sag moment of both halves, so the pinch drops to zero and one arm frees the saw by pulling it up. That is the ordinary way of taking a saw out of a kerf. The second hand adds nothing that a reviewer analysing the easiest route would accept. The undercut-on-cantilever layout does force the second hand: forces at the kerf have almost no moment about the hinge, and pulling the saw down tightens the pinch. But it needs a tree limb, and that layout fails on reach and load (see reach_check).
nearest:
Grepped pipeline/known_tasks.tsv (2,479 rows) for saw|kerf|pinch|branch|prun|limb|lopper|sawhorse|hacksaw|tree|log|firewood|lumber|timber|wedge and for stuck|jam|bind|free|extract|pry|garden|hedge|shear|overhang|cantilever|sag. Also grepped -w saw|branch|kerf|pruning across tasks/*/task.json; none matched (the hits were the ornament stand's dowel branches and bread-loaf sawing). No pinch or kerf recovery task exists, so the idea is novel as a title.
Nearest PRs, read with gh pr view --comments:
- #1381, bucking a log with a two-person crosscut saw: "Not accepted: final" for egregious simplification, because "the log starts in two halves and the blade slides without cutting or resistance". This design also starts the branch as two rigid halves and never cuts, so it invites the same reading.
- #1298, pruning a dead rose stem (revising): the reviewer demanded "blade-cane contact and approximately realistic cutting resistance" and protection for the gripper pads.
- #2302, kerf-in weatherstrip (revising): sent back until a measured real insertion force was modelled. Expect the same demand for pinch force here.
- #1984, clamping a strip in a vise and sawing it (revising): sent back for partial credit and a saw with a round handle.
- #2173, lifting a sagging gate while sliding its bolt: final, as a variant of "hold a misaligned door against a load while engaging a bolt". "Lift the load off while the other hand works" is already an occupied family.
- Accepted neighbours: #1059 (hedge shears, sparing the flowers) and #36 (unloading a cantilevered plank without tipping it). Neither involves freeing a bound tool.
reach_check:
Ran yam_arena.ik.solve and the ArmPlan trajectory check from READY on station.BASES, with top-down grips and TABLE_TOP 0.7475. Every control stayed in its real place. Script: /tmp/claude-1001/-home-mzhang-code-benchmark-tasks/c5e8a00a-04bc-4d39-bc84-61696031f06f/scratchpad/reach_saw2.py.

Layout A (branch along x on two 9.1 cm blocks, cut at x = 0.36, axis at TOP+0.126):
- Right arm, saw handle: grip at (0.36, -0.27, TOP+0.135), yaw +-pi/2, then draw 13 cm along -y, then lift. 0.03 mm and 0.01 degrees at every pose, worst on the trajectory 0.08 mm, limits OK.
- One-arm straight-up shortcut, 6 cm up: reachable at 0.04 mm, with only 0.04 rad left on joint 4. The shortcut is kinematically available.
- Left arm lifting the near half 8 cm from the cut at (0.28, 0, axis+0.013): 0.03-0.04 mm. The hover at TOP+0.18 hits the joint 4 limit (7.7 mm), so hover at TOP+0.16 or lower.
- Left arm lifting the far half at x = 0.44: unreachable top-down (33-38 mm, 7-14 degrees, joint 4 at its limit).

Layout B (in-tree undercut, 5 cm limb along y at TOP+0.25):
- Left arm reaching the saw handle under the limb at (0.15, 0.15): 0.03-0.05 mm.
- Right arm lifting the outer limb at (0.40, -0.10, TOP+0.26): unreachable (20-30 mm, 22 degrees, joint 4 at its limit, both yaw signs).
So the only layout that forces the second hand cannot be reached.
reviewer_reasons:
wide-funnel deepen, 17 Nov: killed. Kill. Reasons, most serious first:
1. The fault as stated is physically wrong. A top cut beside a support with the outer end overhanging opens the kerf (Husqvarna, Dolmar, Milwaukee). Only a cut between two supports, or an undercut on a cantilever, pinches.
2. In the two-support layout the robot can reach, one arm lifting the saw straight up in its own plane lifts the cut region. About 6 N cancels the sag moment, and the saw comes free. The easiest valid route is the ordinary withdrawal, which is our #2400 lesson again.
3. The scale is wrong either way. A 60 cm, 2 kg branch on a bench sags 0.7 N m. Elastically that closes a half-depth kerf by microns, so a real one would not pinch at all, or only lightly (about 9-16 N of friction at a steel-on-wood mu of 0.3-0.5). The sim would need an artificially free hinge: a load scaled down to suit the robot, and an invented pinch. Real pinches come from 1-2 m logs or long limbs, needing 30-100 N of lift near the cut, beyond the YAM (shoulder stiffness 80 N m/rad, effort 27 N m).
4. The in-tree undercut that genuinely forces the second hand puts the lift pose out of top-down reach (joint 4 limit), and it needs a tree on the table.
5. The sim's rigid blade cannot kink. Twisting it would pry the rigid halves apart, an unrealistic shortcut. Banning it needs a 10-degree wrench limit, which reviewers may call invented and which is hard to check from a photo.
6. #1381 was finally rejected for the same pre-split-log, no-cutting model.
7. Lifting a load off with one hand while the other works echoes #2173's rejected family.
8. SimReady has no pruning saw. A 1.5 mm blade in a 2 mm kerf under PhysX's 4 mm contact offset and mu 1.2 risks jitter.
